title: The dark night, again
hookLine: when God seems absent, John says he may be very near
tomorrow: can you yell at God and still be praying?

lines: FROM A BRIGHT KITCHEN TO A DARK PORCH.
cards: Step from a bright kitchen onto a porch at night, and for a moment there's nothing. Then your eyes adjust: the fence, the tree, the shape of the yard. Prayer can go dark like that, except it doesn't adjust.
You pray and feel nothing, for weeks. A Spanish friar, John of the Cross, wrote about exactly that, and his answer is strange: when God seems absent, he may be very near.

teach.h: A SOUL SLIPS OUT ON A DARK NIGHT.
teach.b: John was a Carmelite, and tradition says he wrote some of his poems while locked in a cell by his own brothers. One begins on a dark night, a soul slipping out of a quiet house to meet the one it loves.
In his commentary, John calls dryness in prayer a night: the old warm feelings go quiet, and nothing seems to take their place. Then his surprise.

teach.h: TOO MUCH LIGHT TO SEE BY.
teach.b: The dark, he says, can come from too much light, the way staring at the sun leaves you seeing nothing. The nearness is what blinds.
A psalm says it from the other side, in the Douay-Rheims Bible: "darkness shall not be dark to thee."
Here's one to tell a friend: Mother Teresa's private letters, published after her death, describe a long darkness in her prayer, while she kept serving the poor in Calcutta.
One honest line: a dark night in prayer and depression can look alike. If it's sleep and appetite and hope going too, that's a reason to get help, and help is holy.

how: Catholics who go through dryness in prayer often keep their usual prayers, Mass and the rosary anyway, and some talk it over with a spiritual director or confessor.

o: a night spent awake in prayer before a feast
a stretch where prayer goes dry and God seems far
a season of punishment for a serious sin

games.q: the dark night — tap the pairs.
p: a Spanish friar who wrote of the night
prayer gone dry, God seeming absent

s: "dark night of the soul" just means a really bad day
for John it's a stretch where prayer goes dry and God seems absent, and he trusted God was in it.
John of the Cross thought the dark could come from too much light
like staring at the sun: the nearness is what blinds.
a dark night in prayer and depression are always the same thing
they can look alike; when sleep, appetite and hope go too, get help. help is holy.

games.q: your friend says prayer used to feel warm and now it's dry. she's thinking of quitting, since it "clearly isn't working." what would John of the Cross tell her?
o: the dryness may be God working close by; keep showing up.
warm feelings are the sign God's there; go find them again.
dry prayer means she did something wrong; find it and fix it.
games.why: John taught that the dark can come from too much light: God near, not gone. and if it's more than prayer going dark, help is holy.

practice: Dim the lights or close your eyes, and let the room go dark. Notice what's still there without sight: the chair holding you, the air on your skin, a sound somewhere in the house. Don't try to make it bright.
If you pray, you can say the psalm's line once, darkness shall not be dark to thee, and then just stay, the way John stayed. When the bell rings, open your eyes slowly and watch the room come back.

wordCard.voice: The dark night. John of the Cross's name for prayer gone dry, a night he trusted God was in.

orig.note: Latin, Psalm 138:12 in the Vulgate: darkness shall not be dark to thee.

carryVoice: Here's the line: near in the dark, the way too much light can leave you seeing nothing. See you tomorrow.
